canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: Aims : Dermatopathic reaction is a histopathological finding of lymph nodes that usually occurs in patients with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions. However, it is sometimes seen in patients with cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by infection with human T cell leukaemia virus type I (HTLV-1), which is frequently accompanied by cutaneous lesions. However, the detailed clinicopathological characteristics of the dermatopathic reaction of lymph nodes in ATLL patients and HTLV-1 carriers, addressed in this study, remains to be clarified. Methods and results : We retrospectively analysed 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers. Axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were the primary affected tissues. Three cases with atypical lymphoid cell infiltration were defined as ATLL with dermatopathic reaction (ATLL-D), showing an abnormal T cell immunophenotype and T cell monoclonality. Two of the three ATLL-D patients died 14 and 7 months after diagnosis (the third case had a very short follow-up). The other 15 patients were indistinguishable from reactive lesions and were defined as HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis with dermatopathic reaction (HAL-D). They showed an indolent clinical course, with only one case eventually transforming to aggressive disease.

findings.claim: HAL-D (HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis with dermatopathic reaction) -> 15 of 18 cases; histologically indistinguishable from reactive lesions
findings.verbatim_support: Aims : Dermatopathic reaction is a histopathological finding of lymph nodes that usually occurs in patients with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions. However, it is sometimes seen in patients with cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by infection with human T cell leukaemia virus type I (HTLV-1), which is frequently accompanied by cutaneous lesions. However, the detailed clinicopathological characteristics of the dermatopathic reaction of lymph nodes in ATLL patients and HTLV-1 carriers, addressed in this study, remains to be clarified. Methods and results : We retrospectively analysed 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers. Axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were the primary affected tissues. Three cases with atypical lymphoid cell infiltration were defined as ATLL with dermatopathic reaction (ATLL-D), showing an abnormal T cell immunophenotype and T cell monoclonality. Two of the three ATLL-D patients died 14 and 7 months after diagnosis (the third case had a very short follow-up). The other 15 patients were indistinguishable from reactive lesions and were defined as HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis with dermatopathic reaction (HAL-D). They showed an indolent clinical course, with only one case eventually transforming to aggressive disease.

map_chunks.summary_text: This retrospective study (PMC7383570) examined 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers [S5]. Dermatopathic reaction is a lymph node histopathological finding typically associated with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions [S1] but also occasionally seen in cutaneous T cell lymphoma [S2]. ATLL, caused by HTLV-1, is frequently accompanied by cutaneous lesions [S3]. Axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were the primary affected tissues [S6]. Three cases (ATLL-D) showed atypical lymphoid cell infiltration, abnormal T cell immunophenotype, and T cell monoclonality [S7]; two of these patients died at 7 and 14 months post-diagnosis [S8]. The remaining 15 cases (HAL-D) were histologically indistinguishable from reactive lesions [S9] and followed an indolent clinical course, with only one case transforming to aggressive disease [S10].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes dermatopathic lymphadenopathy (DL) and its relation to cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). DL is characterised morphologically by an expanded paracortex containing interdigitating dendritic cells and pigmented macrophages [S1]. It typically occurs in the context of pruritic cutaneous lesions without malignancy [S2]. However, in CTCL such as mycosis fungoides, nodal dermatopathic lesions may harbour tumour cell infiltration, which has prognostic implications [S3]. Differentiating true lymphomatous involvement from reactive dermatopathic changes is diagnostically challenging because the latter features a polymorphous cellular milieu—including numerous transformed lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and dendritic cells—that can mimic lymphoma [S4].

findings.verbatim_support: Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by infection with human T cell leukaemia virus type I (HTLV-1). map_chunks.summary_text: ATLL is a T cell malignancy caused by HTLV-1 infection [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913], presenting as four clinical subtypes: smouldering, chronic, lymphoma, and acute [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. The lymphoma and acute subtypes are aggressive with a rapid clinical course [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913], while the smouldering and chronic (indolent) subtypes progress slowly without need for cytotoxic chemotherapy [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. Lymphadenopathy is among the most frequent manifestations [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. Morphologically, aggressive-type ATLL shows diffuse architectural effacement with medium-sized or large pleomorphic cells [S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis (HAL), a morphologically reactive lymphadenitis in HTLV-1 carriers, has a good prognosis without treatment [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. While ATLL lymphoma vs. HAL distinction is usually straightforward morphologically, pathological features such as dermatopathic reactions can complicate accurate evaluation of lymph node lesions in HTLV-1 carriers [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913].

findings.claim: Skin involved in up to 50% of ATLL cases
findings.verbatim_support: Although skin is one of the most frequently affected organs in ATLL and may be involved in up to 50% of cases, the detailed clinicopathological findings of ATLL and HAL cases with dermatopathic reaction remain unclear. To address this issue, we carried out a comparative clinicopathological analysis of lymph nodes with dermatopathic reaction in 18 HTLV-1-infected cases with or without ATLL. The majority of these cases were considered to be reactive lesions showing an indolent clinical course, while three cases with definitive involvement by tumour cells showed a relatively poorer prognosis. These findings highlighted the disease spectrum from benign to malignant status in dermatopathic reaction of lymph nodes of HTLV-1 carriers.

map_chunks.summary_text: In this HAL-D case series (PMC7383570), treatment varied by disease subtype: the single smouldering-type case received oral etoposide (VP-16) [S1], while the remaining 14 cases (HTLV-1 carriers or cutaneous-type ATLL) received topical therapy for cutaneous lesions [S1]. Overall, HAL-D demonstrated an indolent clinical course with no definitive transformation in the majority of cases [S2, S5]. One exception was case 12, which progressed to aggressive-type ATLL 30 months after lymph node biopsy and died within 1 month [S3]; pathological review of this case notably failed to identify Hodgkin-Reed-Sternberg (HRS)-like cells, described as a hallmark of incipient ATLL [S4]. Case 5 died 6 years after HAL-D diagnosis from an unknown cause without confirmed transformation [S6], and case 11 (cutaneous type) died from Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia 2 months after biopsy without transformation to aggressive ATLL [S7]. Case 14 presented an unusual finding of EBV-infected atypical large B-cell proliferation [S8] in an 83-year-old patient who was HIV-seronegative and had no documented immunosuppressive status [S9].

In HAL-D, lymph node tissue architecture is preserved, with paracortical expansion featuring proliferating transformed large lymphoid cells and aggregates of interdigitating dendritic cells, Langerhans cells, and macrophages forming mottled clear foci [S1]. Transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli are a universal finding [S2]. CD25-positive cells are numerous throughout the expanded paracortex in all cases by IHC [S3], while the number of CD30-positive cells varies without clear correlation between neoplastic and reactive lesions [S4]. HRS-like cells and CD15-positive large cells are consistently absent [S5]. TCR clonal rearrangement analysis shows a polyclonal pattern in 12 cases, not evaluable in 3 cases, with T-cell monoclonality detected by PCR in only 1 case (case 2), though no definitive atypical tumour cells or T-cell phenotypical abnormalities were identified in that case [S6, S7]. All HAL-D lymph node samples demonstrate a normal T-cell phenotype by flow cytometry and/or IHC [S8].

findings.claim: ATLL-D -> polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate admixed with dendritic cells containing abundant clear cytoplasm
findings.verbatim_support: Cases 16, and 18, classified as ATLL-D, also showed a polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate admixed with dendritic cells containing abundant clear cytoplasm that were positive for S-100 (Figure 2A -F). HAL-D cases generally followed an indolent clinical course, while 2/3 ATLL-D cases showed aggressive behaviour [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21930]; a third ATLL-D case with leukaemic atypical lymphocytes, decreased albumin, and elevated LDH was tentatively classified as unfavourable chronic type with poor prognosis [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21930]. Abnormal T cell immunophenotype (assessed by flow cytometry) was useful for distinguishing HAL-D from ATLL-D and for separating neoplastic from inflammatory status [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21930], and also predicted disease aggressiveness [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21930]. findings.claim: EBV-infected large B cells (in ATLL context) -> CD20 uniformly positive
findings.verbatim_support: In case 14, there was focal proliferation of EBV-infected large B cells, whereas definitive clonal T cell proliferation or abnormal T cell immunophenotype was not observed. This finding has been described in several lymphomas, including angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma, and reflects an immunodeficient local environment created by tumour cells. This case was distinguished from the Hodgkin lymphoma-like variant accompanied by incipient ATLL because the proliferating cells were uniformly positive for CD20 (Figure 5D), focally positive for CD30 and negative for CD15. EBV-positive B cell lymphoproliferative disorders, associated with age-related immune deficiency and comprising a wide disease spectrum from benign to malignant status, is one possibility. However, an immunosuppressive status induced by HTLV-1 infection could also contribute to the proliferation of EBV-infected cells, as previously reported. ATLL tumour cells and HTLV-1-infected cells often exhibit the phenotype of regulatory T cells, including expression of CD4, CD25 and forkhead box P3. EBV-positive cell proliferation combined with dermatopathic reaction mimicking lymphoma-type ATLL can be a potential pitfall in routine diagnosis.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes diagnostic and immunophenotypic features of a case (case 14) involving focal proliferation of EBV-infected large B cells in the setting of ATLL. The proliferating B cells were uniformly CD20+ [S3], focally CD30+ [S3], and CD15– [S3], distinguishing this from the Hodgkin lymphoma-like variant of incipient ATLL. No definitive clonal T cell proliferation or abnormal T cell immunophenotype was identified [S1]. EBV-positive large B cell proliferation is a recognised feature in several T cell lymphomas including angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma, attributed to an immunodeficient local tumour microenvironment [S2]. HTLV-1-induced immunosuppression may further facilitate EBV-infected cell outgrowth [S5]. ATLL tumour cells and HTLV-1-infected cells characteristically express a regulatory T cell phenotype (CD4, CD25, FoxP3) [S6]. EBV-positive B cell lymphoproliferative disorders encompass a spectrum from benign to malignant and are linked to age-related immune deficiency [S4]. Importantly, EBV-positive cell proliferation combined with dermatopathic reaction can mimic lymphoma-type ATLL and represents a diagnostic pitfall [S7].

ATLL lymphoma type is characterised by a very aggressive clinical course and dismal prognosis [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932], and it remains uncertain whether ATLL-D cases should be managed as lymphoma type. The Hodgkin-like ATLL type has been previously described as an incipient form of ATLL [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932]. Although ATLL-D has distinct morphological findings from the Hodgkin-like type [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932], it is proposed as another potential variant of incipient ATLL [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932]. The authors note that further clinicopathological assessment of similar cases is needed to confirm this classification [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932].

map_chunks.summary_text: This concluding chunk (PMC7383570) summarises key findings and clinical recommendations regarding nodal lesions in HTLV-1 carriers [S1]. HTLV-1 carriers present with a spectrum of nodal lesions accompanied by dermatopathic reaction [S1]. HAL-D and ATLLD share overlapping features, and careful assessment of atypical lymphoid cell infiltration, abnormal T cell immunophenotype, and clonality rearrangement is required to distinguish reactive from neoplastic conditions [S2]. Once overt lymphoma has been excluded, HAL-D follows an indolent clinical course [S3]. Treatment of HAL-D should consist of topical therapy, and cytotoxic chemotherapy should be avoided to prevent overtreatment [S4].
